title: Same children, more chikkis: what happens to each child's share?
description: The number of children stays the same while the number of chikkis shared goes up. The board counts pieces of one fractional unit for one fifth and two fifths, then writes one half as four eighths to compare it with five eighths. Keeko doubts the reasoning by saying a bigger top number always means a bigger share.
teaching_notes: One idea: with the same number of children, more units shared means more pieces of the same size for each child. Watch for students who compare top numbers when the bottom numbers differ.

source: Suppose the number of children is kept the same, but the num
video_script.why: A learner sees that with the same number of children, more units shared gives each child more pieces of the same size.
video_script.substitution: the book's own pairs one fifth and two fifths, three sevenths and four sevenths, one half and five eighths
video_script.anchor: chikkis shared among the same number of children, first one chikki and then two chikkis
video_script.wrong_answer: a bigger top number always means a bigger share
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a bigger top number always means a bigger share, which fails when the bottom numbers differ, as in one half and three eighths.

final_answer.value: Each child's share becomes larger: 1/5 < 2/5, 3/7 < 4/7 and 1/2 = 4/8 < 5/8
final_answer.spoken: each child's share becomes larger, because more units are split among the same number of children

video_script.fraction_reading: one fifth, two fifths, three sevenths, four sevenths, one half, five eighths
never_show: a bigger top number always wins
maths_rules: 1 chikki among 5 children gives 1/5 each; 2 chikkis among the same 5 children give 2/5 each
same number of children means the same fractional unit, 1/5
2/5 has 2 pieces of 1/5 and 1/5 has 1 piece, so 1/5 < 2/5
3/7 has 3 pieces of 1/7 and 4/7 has 4 pieces, so 3/7 < 4/7
1/2 = (1 x 4)/(2 x 4) = 4/8, and 4/8 has 4 pieces of 1/8, 5/8 has 5 pieces, so 1/2 < 5/8
slip: Keeko says a bigger top number always means a bigger share; but 3 is bigger than 1 and 3/8 < 1/2, because 1/2 = 4/8
video_script.design: Five children share first one chikki and then two chikkis, and pieces of one fifth are counted. Then one half is written as four eighths for the last pair.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks a bigger top number always means a bigger share.
<bookmark mark='test'/>That works only when the bottom numbers match. Take one half and three eighths. Three is bigger than one.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Yet one half is four eighths, so three eighths is less. We must look at the bottom number too.
